974.title: The Anand Marriage Act, 1909
974.hook: the law recognizes Sikh weddings around the Granth
974.howItsDone: Sikh weddings are performed as Anand Karaj: the couple sits before the Guru Granth Sahib, and as each of the four lavan is read and then sung, they walk around the Granth, usually in the morning, in the presence of the sangat.

segments.voice: Yesterday, diwan, and your line was working together. Did you coordinate with someone on something you'd both been doing alone? Today, a new week, and one of the causes the reformers worked on: a wedding. Day nine hundred seventy-four.

A morning wedding in a gurdwara. The bride and groom sit before the Guru Granth Sahib. A hymn is read, then sung, and the couple rises and walks slowly around the Granth, the groom a step ahead, a scarf joining them. Four times, four hymns. Families are crying and laughing at once. And then a question nobody in the room is thinking about: does the law count this as a marriage? For a while, that wasn't certain. Today: the Anand Marriage Act.
screen: `AROUND THE GURU GRANTH SAHIB.` → `FOUR HYMNS, FOUR ROUNDS.` → `DOES THE LAW COUNT IT?`

segments.voice: First, the name. Anand means bliss. A Sikh wedding is called Anand Karaj, the ceremony of bliss. At its heart are the lavan, four hymns of Guru Ram Das in Rag Suhi. Laav means a round. As each one is sung, the couple walks one round around the Guru Granth Sahib. Second, what the hymns say. They're not about a bride and groom alone. In the lavan, the soul is the bride and the Lord is the beloved. The first round speaks of taking up a life of duty and the Name. Later rounds move through love, detachment and, finally, a deep peace, the bride meeting her Lord. A wedding, in Sikh understanding, is two people walking that spiritual path together. Third, the problem. In the reform years, some Sikh weddings still followed the rite of circling a sacred fire, a custom Sikhs shared with their Hindu neighbors. The Singh Sabha reformers urged Anand Karaj as the Sikh way. But some people worried: if a wedding around the Granth had no standing in British law, could it be challenged? Could a widow or a child lose an inheritance? Fourth, the answer. The reformers pressed for a law, and the Anand Marriage Act recognized weddings performed by Anand Karaj as valid. It's a short law. What it protected was large: the right of Sikh couples to marry by the Gurus' hymns and be sure the marriage stood. The lavan recognized, and the families in the room could cry and laugh without a worry behind it.

segments.voice: Two minutes for a couple. Sit, and let your breath slow. Bring to mind a couple you know: newly married, married for decades, or about to be. Picture them side by side, walking slowly, one a step ahead, still connected. Wish them, silently, the things the lavan walk through: steadiness, love, a little freedom from ego, and peace. Breathe slowly with them in mind. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. After the bell, send them a word of congratulation. The bell holds the time.
Anand Karaj, the ceremony of bliss, the Sikh wedding: a law recognized it, the couple walking around the Guru Granth Sahib as the lavan are sung. Today's word.
Your line: the lavan recognized. Today, congratulate one couple, on a wedding, an anniversary, or just on still walking together. Day nine hundred seventy-four.

975.title: Presses and papers
975.hook: Gurmukhi newspapers and presses spread the reform
975.howItsDone: Sikh newspapers, magazines and publishers still print in Gurmukhi and English, and gurdwaras often keep free booklets on Sikh history and practice for visitors to take home.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Anand Karaj, and your line was the lavan recognized. Did you congratulate a couple? Today, how word of causes like that one traveled from town to town. Day nine hundred seventy-five.

Ink on fingers. In a back room in Lahore, a typesetter picks small metal letters out of a wooden case, one by one, and lines them up in a frame. They're Gurmukhi letters, the same shapes a reader meets on a page of the Granth. A lever comes down, the press clanks, and a sheet lifts off with the ink still wet. Soon it will be folded, bundled, and carried to another town. Today: presses and papers.
screen: `METAL LETTERS, SET BY HAND.` → `THE SHAPES OF THE GRANTH.` → `A SHEET, STILL WET.`

segments.voice: First, the script. Gurmukhi is the alphabet the Gurus used for their hymns; tradition credits Guru Angad with shaping it for Sikh use. To print in Gurmukhi was to print in the letters of the Granth. A newspaper set in that type could double as a reading lesson for the scripture. Second, the papers. Reformers started newspapers in Punjabi. The Khalsa Akhbar came out of Lahore, linked to the scholar Giani Ditt Singh. In Amritsar, Bhai Vir Singh, the poet you met a few days ago, ran the Khalsa Samachar. They carried news, arguments about reform, explanations of Sikh history and practice, and appeals for schools and causes. Third, the tracts. Alongside the papers came small, cheap booklets on single subjects: a Guru's life, the meaning of a hymn, how to hold a ceremony. Vir Singh helped found a society to publish them. A tract could be bought for a coin, read in an evening, passed to a neighbor. Fourth, why print mattered. The Gurus had gathered their hymns into a book so the word could be kept and shared. Near the end of the Granth, Guru Arjan speaks of a dish holding truth, contentment and reflection, and Sikh tradition hears that dish as the Granth itself. Print was another way of laying that dish out for everyone. A movement of a few learned men became a conversation in many households. Arguments still broke out, sometimes fierce ones, but they broke out among people who were reading. Print spreads it, and what it spread was not only news but a habit: Sikhs reading their own story in their own letters.

segments.voice: Two minutes with a shape on a page. Sit, and let your breath settle. Bring to mind one Punjabi word you already know from this path: Waheguru, sangat, seva, langar, Khalsa. 976.title: The Rakab Ganj wall
976.hook: the demolition of a gurdwara wall in Delhi stirred protest
976.howItsDone: Gurdwara Rakab Ganj Sahib in New Delhi is visited by Sikhs and others who come to remember Guru Tegh Bahadur, listen to kirtan and eat in the langar; it is remembered alongside Gurdwara Sis Ganj, where the Guru was executed.

segments.voice: Yesterday, akhbar, and your line was print spreads it. Did you read one Punjabi word in its own letters? Today, news that the papers carried quickly, about a wall in Delhi. Day nine hundred seventy-six.

Workmen arrive at a gurdwara in Delhi with orders and tools. A new capital is being laid out nearby, with grand avenues and government buildings, and the gurdwara's outer wall is in the way of the plan. The wall comes down. On paper, it's a small thing: some bricks, a boundary, a straighter line on a map. But the place inside that wall is where, Sikhs remember, a Guru's body was cremated in secret, at great risk, by people who loved him. Today: the Rakab Ganj wall.
screen: `WORKMEN WITH ORDERS.` → `A WALL IN THE WAY OF A PLAN.` → `WHAT THE WALL ENCLOSED.`

segments.voice: First, the place. Gurdwara Rakab Ganj stands where, tradition says, the body of Guru Tegh Bahadur was cremated after his execution in Delhi. Sikhs remember him as the Guru who gave his life rather than see others forced from their faith. Tradition remembers a trader with a train of ox-carts, Lakhi Shah Vanjara, carrying the body away under cover of a storm and setting fire to his own house so the Guru could be cremated without the authorities knowing. A house burned to honor a Guru. That's what the ground means. Second, the wall. When the British laid out the new capital, an outer wall of the gurdwara was knocked down to fit the plan. To the planners it was a boundary. To Sikhs it was the edge of holy ground, and taking it down without care felt like contempt for the Guru's memory. Third, the protest. Sikhs wrote, petitioned and met, and the papers you heard about yesterday spread the news. Some argued for caution and patience. Others insisted that a Sikh holy place couldn't be treated this way and that the community had to stand up. The wall became a test of whether Sikhs could protect their own sacred places. In the end, the wall was rebuilt. Fourth, why a wall matters. The Gurus taught that the Divine is everywhere, not trapped in bricks. Yet Sikhs honor places where the Gurus lived and gave their lives, because memory needs somewhere to stand. A wall says: here, something happened that we won't let anyone forget. The wall mattered, and the protest over it pointed toward bigger struggles to come.

segments.voice: Two minutes for a small sacred thing. Sit, and let your breath slow. Bring to mind one small thing that's sacred to you or to someone you love: a prayer book, a photograph, a grave, a corner of a room, a ring, a gutka with worn pages. Picture it clearly. Notice how easily it could be moved, thrown out, or treated carelessly by someone who doesn't know what it means. Breathe slowly with it. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. After the bell, do one thing to protect it. The bell holds the time.

977.title: Ghadar, 1913
977.hook: Sikh workers in North America founded a party to free India
977.howItsDone: Sikhs in North America and in Punjab remember the Ghadar movement as part of their community's history abroad, and its story is told in gurdwaras, museums and community events, especially among the diaspora on the Pacific coast.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kandh, and your line was the wall mattered. Was there one small sacred thing you guarded? Today, the story leaves Punjab and crosses an ocean. Day nine hundred seventy-seven.

A sawmill on the Pacific coast. The shift is over, the saws go quiet, and a group of men in turbans sit down together on wooden crates. They cut timber and work farm rows for low pay, a long way from their villages. Someone has a newspaper printed in Gurmukhi and Urdu. Someone reads it aloud, because not everyone can read. The talk is not about wages. It's about home: a land under a foreign government, and whether men this far away can still do something for it. Today: Ghadar.
screen: `A SAWMILL ON THE PACIFIC COAST.` → `A NEWSPAPER READ ALOUD.` → `THE TALK IS OF HOME.`

segments.voice: First, the people. Punjabi migrants, many of them Sikh, had gone to Canada and the United States to work in mills, on railways and on farms. Abroad, they met hard treatment, and some of them began to ask why their own country was not free to protect them. Second, the party. In 1913 they founded an organization on the American West Coast to work for India's freedom from British rule. Sohan Singh Bhakna is remembered as one of its leaders, alongside the scholar Har Dayal. Its newspaper was called Ghadar, and soon the movement was known by that name too. The word is usually given as revolt, or uprising. Third, the mix. The Ghadar movement was not a Sikh religious body. Its members were Sikh, Hindu and Muslim, and its papers spoke of India as a whole. But Sikh workers filled its ranks, and gurdwaras abroad were places where its members met. Fourth, the longing. Tradition says Guru Arjan wrote these lines while he was sent away from his father, the Guru. He sings of a mind that longs to see the Guru, the way a thirsty bird longs for rain. Those verses, at Ang 96 of the Guru Granth Sahib, are about longing for the Guru, not for a country. But they show something the hymn says plainly: distance doesn't cancel love. It can sharpen it. The Ghadar workers were an ocean away from Punjab, and their care for it did not fade. That's today's line.
screen: `PUNJABI WORKERS ABROAD.` · `A PARTY FOR INDIA'S FREEDOM.` · `SIKH, HINDU AND MUSLIM MEMBERS.` · `DISTANCE SHARPENS LONGING.` · then, large: `FAR AWAY, STILL CARING.`

Ghadar. A word usually given as revolt; the name of a newspaper, and of a movement of Punjabi workers in North America who worked to free India. Today's word.
Your line: far away, still caring. Today, send a message to someone who lives far from home, and ask how things are where they come from. Day nine hundred seventy-seven.

978.title: Kartar Singh Sarabha
978.hook: a young Ghadar leader executed in 1915 at nineteen
978.howItsDone: Kartar Singh Sarabha is honored across Punjab as a martyr of the freedom struggle; his village of Sarabha holds memorials to him, and his name is given to schools, streets and events.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ghadar, the workers on the Pacific coast, and your line was far away, still caring. Who did you send a message to? Today, one of those workers by name. Day nine hundred seventy-eight.

Sarabha is a village near Ludhiana, and in Punjab the name now belongs to a young man as much as to the place. Schools and roads carry it. He left that village to study in America, and he came back with a cause he would not put down. He traveled the roads of Punjab, talking to anyone who would listen. He didn't live long. The people who remember him call him by his village: Kartar Singh Sarabha.
screen: `A VILLAGE NEAR LUDHIANA.` → `A STUDENT IN AMERICA.` → `A NAME ON SCHOOLS AND ROADS.`

segments.voice: First, the student. Kartar Singh went to the United States to study, and there he met the Ghadar workers from yesterday. He threw himself into the movement, and he's remembered for working on its newspaper, setting the type and getting copies out. Second, the return. When the war in Europe began, the Ghadar movement called its members home to raise a revolt in India. Kartar Singh went back to Punjab and traveled from place to place, trying to win soldiers and villagers to the cause. The plan was discovered, and its members were arrested. Third, the trial. He was tried in Lahore, and in 1915 he was hanged. The Sikh and Punjabi histories that remember him give his age as nineteen. Accounts say he made no effort to save himself in court, and spoke openly of what he had done. Fourth, the Guru's line. Guru Nanak, in a verse at Ang 1412 of the Guru Granth Sahib, says that whoever wishes to play the game of love should come to the Guru's lane with their head on the palm of their hand. In Sikh memory that verse is about giving everything, holding nothing back. Kartar Singh's cause was a political one, not a religious mission, and he is honored well beyond the Sikh community. But the picture of a young man holding his own life out in his open hand is why that verse comes to mind when his name is spoken. One word sits at the center of his story, and it is a number. That's today's line.
screen: `A STUDENT JOINS THE MOVEMENT.` · `HOME TO PUNJAB, AND ARRESTED.` · `TRIED IN LAHORE, HANGED.` · `HEAD ON THE PALM OF THE HAND.` · then, large: `NINETEEN.`

979.title: Budge Budge, 1914
979.hook: the Komagata Maru's passengers returned to India and many were shot on arrival
979.howItsDone: Sikhs remember the Komagata Maru and the Budge Budge shootings as part of their community's history; there are memorials at Budge Budge and in Vancouver, and the passengers are recalled in gurdwaras and community gatherings.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kartar Singh Sarabha, and your line was nineteen. Did you take a young person seriously for one full conversation? Today, a ship that came home to the wrong welcome. Day nine hundred seventy-nine.

A ship lies at anchor in Vancouver harbor. On board are passengers from Punjab, Sikh, Muslim and Hindu, who have paid to cross an ocean for work. Canada will not let them land. For weeks they wait on deck, short of food and water, looking at a shore they can see and cannot reach. At last the ship is forced to turn around. Its name is the Komagata Maru. The long voyage back ends at a riverside landing near Calcutta, called Budge Budge. And the welcome waiting there is worse than the one they left.
screen: `A SHIP HELD IN VANCOUVER HARBOR.` → `A SHORE THEY CAN SEE, NOT REACH.` → `BACK TO A LANDING NEAR CALCUTTA.`

segments.voice: First, the voyage. A Sikh businessman, Gurdit Singh, chartered the Komagata Maru to carry Punjabi migrants to Canada. Canadian rules were written to keep them out, and the passengers were refused. They were turned away once. Second, the landing. When the ship reached Budge Budge in 1914, the British authorities, who suspected the passengers of ties to the Ghadar movement, wanted to put them straight onto a train for Punjab. Accounts say the passengers wanted to go into Calcutta instead, and some set out walking, carrying the Guru Granth Sahib with them. Third, the shooting. Police and troops confronted them, and there was firing. Passengers were killed, others were wounded, and others were arrested. Gurdit Singh escaped and went into hiding. Having been refused by Canada, they were now refused even the freedom to walk where they chose in their own country. Turned away twice. Fourth, the Guru's cry. When Babur's armies fell on the towns of Punjab, Guru Nanak sang a hymn of protest, at Ang 360 of the Guru Granth Sahib. He asks the Creator, in grief: there was such slaughter, such crying out; did You feel no pain? The Babarvani hymns don't explain suffering away. They name it, and they bring it before God. Sikhs remember Budge Budge with a memorial at the landing, and they remember it in that spirit: not hiding the wound, naming it.

If you pray, you can pray for them in your own way, or say Waheguru on each breath out. If you don't, simply keep them company in your thoughts. The bell holds the time.
Budge Budge. The landing near Calcutta where the Komagata Maru's passengers came home, and where police fired on them. Today's word.

980.title: The robe for the general
980.hook: after Jallianwala, the Golden Temple's managers honored the general responsible, and Sikhs were outraged
980.howItsDone: In gurdwaras a siropa, a length of cloth, is given as a mark of honor to a worshipper, a guest or a volunteer; Sikhs remember the siropa given to General Dyer as a wrong that helped start the Gurdwara reform movement.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Budge Budge, and your line was turned away twice. Did you make room for someone shut out? Today, the end of the week, and an honor given to the wrong man. Day nine hundred eighty.

Jallianwala Bagh is a walled garden in Amritsar, a short walk from the Golden Temple. In 1919 a crowd gathered there, and a British general, Reginald Dyer, brought troops in and ordered them to fire on it. The garden had few ways out. When the shooting stopped, the dead and wounded lay across the ground. Soon after, something happened a few minutes' walk away that is hard to tell. The general was honored at the Golden Temple itself. Today: the robe for the general.
screen: `A WALLED GARDEN IN AMRITSAR.` → `A GENERAL ORDERS TROOPS TO FIRE.` → `THEN, AN HONOR.`

segments.voice: First, who was in charge. At that time the Golden Temple was run by a manager appointed under British rule, Arur Singh, along with priests who answered to him, not to the Sikh community. Second, the robe. Accounts say Dyer was received at the Golden Temple and presented with a siropa, the robe or scarf of honor that a gurdwara gives to someone it wishes to honor. Some accounts add that he was declared a Sikh. The man who had ordered the firing was given the gift meant for the honored. Third, the outrage. Sikhs were furious, and not only at Dyer. They asked a harder question: how could the people managing the Golden Temple itself do this? If the managers answered to the government rather than to the Sangat, then the Sangat had to take its gurdwaras back. That anger became one of the sparks of the Gurdwara reform movement, which fills the coming weeks of this path. Fourth, what honor is for. Guru Nanak, at Ang 15 of the Guru Granth Sahib, says he stands with the lowest of the low, and that where the lowly are cared for, there God's grace falls. Read beside this story, the verse puts honor near those who suffer, not with the one who made them suffer. Look back over this week: a wedding law, the printing presses, a gurdwara wall, the Ghadar workers, a nineteen-year-old, and a ship turned away. Again and again, the question underneath was who decides what is sacred, and who is honored. Today, outrage became reform.
screen: `A MANAGER APPOINTED UNDER BRITISH RULE.` · `THE SIROPA GIVEN TO DYER.` · `WHO DO THE MANAGERS ANSWER TO?` · `GRACE FALLS WHERE THE LOWLY ARE CARED FOR.` · then, large: `OUTRAGE BECAME REFORM.`

segments.voice: Two minutes with a wrong honor. Sit, and let your breath slow. Bring to mind one time you saw praise go to the wrong place: credit taken by someone who didn't earn it, or applause for something that hurt people. Notice what rises in you, and let it settle without feeding it. Then ask one quiet question: what would it look like to speak up, calmly, once? You don't have to answer out loud. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Siropa, the robe or length of cloth a gurdwara gives as a mark of honor: given to General Dyer after Jallianwala Bagh, and the outrage that followed. Today's word.
Your line: outrage became reform. Today, if you see credit or praise going to the wrong place, say so once, calmly and plainly. Day nine hundred eighty.

fork.setup: you're a Sikh in Amritsar. you hear the managers of the Golden Temple have honored the general who ordered the firing. what do Sikhs do?
options: accept it; the managers know best.
ask who the managers answer to, and set out to reclaim the gurdwaras.
stop going to the Golden Temple.

trapdoor: what you thought: a robe is just a gift.
what it means: the siropa given to the general who ordered the firing at Jallianwala Bagh, by managers appointed under British rule.
what a scholar hears: the question of who controls the gurdwaras: the outrage turned into a movement to put them back in the Sangat's hands.
